title: Three strangers at Mamre (Genesis 18:1–15)
hookLine: Abraham runs to feed three visitors, and Sarah laughs behind the tent

lines: NOON, IN THE HEAT OF THE DAY.
cards: The hottest part of the day, in the hill country near Hebron. Nobody travels at noon if they can help it. Abraham, with the new name God has given him, is sitting at the door of his tent by the great trees of Mamre.
He's ninety-nine years old. He looks up, and there are three men standing near him. Strangers.
No warning, no dust cloud on the road. Just there. What he does next turns a hot afternoon into a feast.

teach.b: He runs. A ninety-nine-year-old man, in the heat, runs to meet them and bows to the ground.

And then listen to how modest his offer is, in the King James Bible: "Let a little water, I pray you, be fetched, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree: And I will fetch a morsel of bread."
A little water, a morsel of bread. And then he hurries. He tells Sarah to make cakes from a huge amount of fine flour.
He runs to the herd for a tender calf. Butter, milk, meat.
A morsel turns into a feast, and he stands by them under the tree while they eat. Then one of them asks: where is Sarah thy wife? And promises that by this time next year, Sarah will have a son.
Sarah is listening behind the tent door. She's around ninety. And she laughs, quietly, to herself: worn out as I am, and my husband old, shall I have this pleasure now?
The visitor hears it. Why did Sarah laugh? And then the question at the center of today: "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?"
In Hebrew, too hard is too wonderful, from the word pele, a wonder, beyond reach. Sarah, afraid, says I didn't laugh. The answer: "Nay; but thou didst laugh."

teach.h: IS ANY THING TOO HARD FOR THE LORD?
teach.b: The text moves between three men and the LORD speaking. Some Christian readers have seen a hint of the Trinity here; Andrei Rublev's Orthodox icon paints the three seated around one table.
Jewish tradition reads the three as angels, with God appearing to Abraham. And the New Testament letter to the Hebrews draws its own lesson: some have entertained angels unawares.

how: Hospitality to strangers is a long Christian practice, from monasteries that receive every guest as Christ to churches that run open tables, and Rublev's icon of the three visitors hangs in many Orthodox homes and churches.

a quiet laugh of doubt, kept inside

games.q: you're ninety-nine, resting at your tent door at noon. three strangers appear. what do you do?
o: stay seated and wait to see what they want.
run to meet them, bow, and offer a little water and bread.
call your servants to send them on.
games.why: he runs, in the heat, and his "morsel of bread" turns into cakes, a calf, butter and milk.

practice: Think of the next person who'll come to your door, your desk or your table, and picture Abraham's way of meeting them: getting up, going to meet them, offering water before they ask, something to eat, a place to sit.
Small, but more than they expect. If you pray, you can pray for whoever comes next.

wordCard.voice: Pele. Hebrew for a wonder, beyond reach, as in is anything too wonderful for the Lord: the promise Sarah laughed to hear, too wonderful to believe.

orig.note: Hebrew: a wonder. Is anything too hard for the LORD? is, in Hebrew, is anything too wonderful.

carryVoice: Your line: is anything too hard? A morsel of bread can turn into a feast. Day three hundred fifty-three, done.
